questions.problem:
Anna decides to go jogging. Her position from the starting point, measured in meters, is given by the function $s(t),$ where $t$ is the time in seconds. The values of $s(t)$ for different values of $t$ are given in the table below:

| **$t$** | $1$ | $3$ | $5$ | $7$ | $9$ | $11$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $s(t)$ | $1$ | $2$ | $4$ | $6$ | $14$ | $25$ |

$$

$$

Approximate the velocity ${s}^{′}(t)$ at the point $t=7$ using a central difference approximation with the step size $h=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
We use the central difference approximation

$$
{s}^{′}(t)≈\frac{s(t+h)-s(t-h)}{2h},
$$

 
at the time $t=7$ with step size $h=2.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}^{′}(7) & ≈\frac{s(7+2)-s(7-2)}{2(2)} \\  & =\frac{s(9)-s(5)}{2(2)} \\  & =\frac{14-4}{4} \\  & =\frac{10}{4} \\  & =2.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the velocity of Anna at the instant of time $t=7$ is $2.5\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

questions.problem: What is ${\int }_{4}^{9}\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x$ expressed as the limit of a right Riemann sum?
questions.worked_solution:
The definite integral can be defined in terms of the limit of a right Riemann sum as

$$
{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx,
$$

where ${x}_{k}=a+kΔx$ and $Δx=\frac{b-a}{n}.$

In the definite integral

$$
{\int }_{4}^{9}\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x,
$$

the function is $f(x)=\sqrt{x},$ the lower bound is $a=4$ and the upper bound is $b=9.$ So, we have

$$
Δx=\frac{9-4}{n}=\frac{5}{n}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{4}^{9}\sqrt{x}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}f({x}_{k})\cdot Δx \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(4+k\cdot \frac{5}{n})\cdot \frac{5}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[f(4+\frac{5k}{n})\cdot \frac{5}{n}] \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{\sum }_{k=1}^{n}[\sqrt{4+\frac{5k}{n}}\cdot \frac{5}{n}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that $f(x)=\frac{2{x}^{2}+3x-2}{4-{x}^{2}},$ which of the following statements is correct?

I. ${lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x)=-\infty $

II. ${lim}_{x\to (-2)^{+}}f(x)=\infty $

III. ${lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x)=-\infty $
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's factor the numerator and denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{2{x}^{2}+3x-2}{4-{x}^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{(x+2)(2x-1)}{(x-2)(x+2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain is  $x\ne \pm 2,$ and we notice that the function can be simplified:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x)=-\frac{2x-1}{x-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we see that the function has the only vertical asymptote $x=2.$ So statement II is false.

To find  ${lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x)$ and ${lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x),$ we evaluate $f(x)$ at $x$-values very close to $x=2$ from the left and right.

| $x$ | $1.99$ | $1.999$ | $2$ | $2.001$ | $2.01$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $298$ | $2\,998$ | $\text{undefined}$ | $-3\,002$ | $-302$ |

All values are positive and get larger and larger as $x\to 2$ from the left and all values are negative and get smaller and smaller as $x\to 2$ from the right . Therefore, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to {2}^{+}}f(x)=-\infty \,{lim}_{x\to {2}^{-}}f(x)=\infty 
$$

Consequently, statement I is true and III is false.

In conclusion, only statement I is correct. A plot of the function is shown below.

questions.problem: Find the real solution to the equation $4\operatorname{sinh}⁡x=-3.$
questions.worked_solution:
The definition of $\operatorname{sinh}⁡x$ is

$$
\operatorname{sinh}⁡x=\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}).
$$

Substituting the above definition into the equation $4\operatorname{sinh}⁡x=-3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot (\frac{1}{2}({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x})) & =-3 \\ 2({e}^{x}-{e}^{-x}) & =-3 \\ 2{e}^{x}-2{e}^{-x} & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we multiply both sides of the equation by ${e}^{x},$ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}\cdot (2{e}^{x}-2{e}^{-x}) & ={e}^{x}\cdot (-3) \\ 2{e}^{2x}-2 & =-3{e}^{x} \\ 2{e}^{2x}+3{e}^{x}-2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This is a quadratic equation in ${e}^{x}$ that we can factor as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2{e}^{x}-1)({e}^{x}+2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

By the zero-product property, we have to solve two equations:

$$
2{e}^{x}-1=0,\,{e}^{x}+2=0
$$

Solving the two equations above for $x,$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{e}^{x}-1 & =0 &  & \, & {e}^{x}+2 & =0 \\ {e}^{x} & =\frac{1}{2} &  & \, & {e}^{x} & =-2 \\ x & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2}) &  & \, & \end{aligned}
$$

There are no real values of $x$ for which ${e}^{x}=-2.$ Therefore, $x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{2})$ is the only real solution to the equation.

questions.problem: Evaluate ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{x}{x-1})}^{3x-3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that as $x\to \infty ,$ 

- the expression inside the parentheses approaches $1,$ while

- the exponent approaches $\infty .$

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{x}{x-1})}^{3x-3}={1}^{\infty },
$$

which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit:

$$
{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}=e
$$

We rewrite the given limit as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{x}{x-1})}^{3x-3} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{(x-1)+1}{x-1})}^{3x-3} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{x-1})}^{3(x-1)}\end{aligned}
$$

Let $x-1=n.$ Therefore, since $n\to \infty $ as $x\to \infty ,$ we rewrite the limit using the algebra of limits, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{x}{x-1})}^{3x-3} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{x-1})}^{3(x-1)} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{3n} \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }{[{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{3} \\  & ={[{lim}_{n\to \infty }{(1+\frac{1}{n})}^{n}]}^{3} \\  & ={e}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find all of the points where the function $f(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}+3x}{{x}^{2}+4x+3}$ has discontinuities due to vertical asymptotes.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the vertical asymptotes, let's start by factoring the expressions in the numerator and denominator. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{2}+3x}{{x}^{2}+4x+3} \\  & =\frac{x(x+3)}{(x+1)(x+3)} \\  & =\frac{x\cancel{(x+3)}}{(x+1)\cancel{(x+3)}} \\  & =\frac{x}{x+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the vertical asymptotes, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve:

$$
x+1=0\,⟹\,x=-1
$$

Therefore, the function has a discontinuity due to a vertical asymptote at $x=-1$ only.

questions.problem:
Let $f(x)$ be the function defined below. For what value of $k$ is $f(x)$ continuous at $x=-1?$

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{k}{x-1}, & x<-1 \\ 2x-k, & x\ge -1\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
From the definition of $f(x)$, the left-sided limit of $f(x)$ at $x=-1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -{1}^{-}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to -{1}^{-}}\frac{k}{x-1} \\  & =\frac{k}{-1-1} \\  & =-\frac{k}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, the right-sided limit is

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -{1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to -{1}^{+}}(2x-k) \\  & =2(-1)-k \\  & =-2-k.\end{aligned}
$$

We also note that $f(-1)=-2-k.$ 

So, for $f(x)$ to be continuous at $x=-1,$ we must have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -{1}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to -{1}^{-}}f(x) \\ -2-k & =-\frac{k}{2} \\ -4-2k & =-k \\ k & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $k=-4$ removes the discontinuity at $x=-1.$

questions.problem:
Suppose that $f(x)$ is defined as

$$
f(x)=\{\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x, & x\le 0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡x, & x>0.\end{aligned}
$$

On which of the following intervals can the extreme value theorem be applied to the function?

I. $[-2,-1]$

II. $[-1,1]$

III. $(0,1]$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that the extreme value theorem is only applicable to closed intervals on which the function is continuous.

So, let's check whether the function is continuous on each of the intervals.

- First, consider $[-2,-1].$ In this interval, $f(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and so $f(x)$ is continuous on $[-2,-1].$  Therefore, the extreme value theorem is applicable on this interval.

- Now, consider the interval $[-1,1].$ In this case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to {0}^{+}}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)=-\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x)$ has an essential discontinuity at $x=0.$ Therefore, $f(x)$ is not continuous on the interval $[-1,1],$ and the extreme value theorem is not applicable on this interval.

- Finally, we note that the interval $(0,1]$ is not closed, so the extreme value theorem is not applicable.

In conclusion, the correct answer is "I only".

questions.problem:
The functions $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ are twice-differentiable on an open interval containing $x=1.$ The values of $f,$ $g,$ and their respective derivatives are given below:

| $x$ | $f(x)$ | ${f}^{′}(x)$ | ${f}^{″}(x)$ | $g(x)$ | ${g}^{′}(x)$ | ${g}^{″}(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $1$ | $-1$ | $-1$ | $4$ | $1$ | $1$ | $-2$ |

$$

$$

Find ${lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{f(x)+x}{g(x)-x}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that if we try to substitute $x=1$ directly into the limit, we reach the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{f(x)+x}{g(x)-x} & ={\frac{f(x)+x}{g(x)-x}|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{f(1)+1}{g(1)-1} \\  & =\frac{-1+1}{1-1} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

So, we use L'Hopital's rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{f(x)+x}{g(x)-x} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{(f(x)+x)^{′}}{(g(x)-x)^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{′}(x)+1}{{g}^{′}(x)-1}\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=1$ again, but once more, we reach the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{′}(x)+1}{{g}^{′}(x)-1} & ={\frac{{f}^{′}(x)+1}{{g}^{′}(x)-1}|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{{f}^{′}(1)+1}{{g}^{′}(1)-1} \\  & =\frac{-1+1}{1-1} \\  & =\frac{0}{0}\end{aligned}
$$

We apply L'Hopital's rule again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{′}(x)+1}{{g}^{′}(x)-1} & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{({f}^{′}(x)+1)^{′}}{({g}^{′}(x)-1)^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{″}(x)}{{g}^{″}(x)},\end{aligned}
$$

and this time, when we substitute $x=1,$ we are actually able to determine the result:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{{f}^{″}(x)}{{g}^{″}(x)} & ={\frac{{f}^{″}(x)}{{g}^{″}(x)}|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{{f}^{″}(1)}{{g}^{″}(1)} \\  & =\frac{4}{-2} \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${lim}_{x\to 1}\frac{f(x)+x}{g(x)-x}=-2.$

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the ellipse shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
Since our ellipse is centered at $(-1,2)$ and has semiaxes $4$ and $2,$ its equation is given by

$$
\frac{(x-(-1))^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1\,⟹\,\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{16}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{4}=1.
$$

Now, to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{16}+\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{4}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{(x+1)^{2}}{16})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{(y-2)^{2}}{4}) & =0 \\ \frac{2(x+1)}{16}+\frac{2(y-2)}{4}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ \frac{y-2}{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x+1}{8} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{x+1}{4(y-2)}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the function $y=\sqrt{({x}^{2}+6x){sin}^{2}⁡x}.$  The derivative of this function for $x\in (0,\pi )$ is given by

$$
{y}^{′}=\frac{g(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+h(x)\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+6x}}.
$$

Find the function $g(x)+h(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
Our function can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+6x){sin}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+6x}\cdot \sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =({x}^{2}+6x)^{1/2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we take the natural logarithm of both sides and use the product and power rules for logarithms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+6x)^{1/2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(({x}^{2}+6x)^{1/2})+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡y & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+6x)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we differentiate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡y) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+6x)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)) \\ \frac{1}{y}\cdot {y}^{′} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}+6x}\cdot (2x+6)+\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{{y}^{′}}{y} & =\frac{x+3}{{x}^{2}+6x}+\operatorname{cot}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve for ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y(\frac{x+3}{{x}^{2}+6x}+\operatorname{cot}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute $y=\sqrt{({x}^{2}+6x){sin}^{2}⁡x}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+6x){sin}^{2}⁡x}(\frac{x+3}{{x}^{2}+6x}+\operatorname{cot}⁡x) \\  & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+6x){sin}^{2}⁡x}(\frac{x+3}{{x}^{2}+6x}+\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}) \\  & =\sqrt{({x}^{2}+6x){sin}^{2}⁡x}(\frac{(x+3)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+({x}^{2}+6x)\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{({x}^{2}+6x)\operatorname{sin}⁡x}) \\  & =\frac{|\operatorname{sin}⁡x|}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\frac{(x+3)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+({x}^{2}+6x)\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+6x}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Given that $x\in (0,\pi ),$ then $|\operatorname{sin}⁡x|=\operatorname{sin}⁡x,$ so the fraction $\frac{|\operatorname{sin}⁡x|}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}$ simplifies to $1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{(x+3)\operatorname{sin}⁡x+({x}^{2}+6x)\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+6x}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
g(x)+h(x)=x+3+{x}^{2}+6x={x}^{2}+7x+3.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14188718/assets/63fe9cf3a61a5cef09f9c19e16a18318338faa6837eeb77b83f49b636157bb95.png)

A sphere is decreasing in volume at a rate of $54\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}\text{/s}.$ Calculate the rate at which the radius of the sphere is decreasing at the moment when the radius is $3\,\text{cm}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of the balloon and $V$ its volume. Both $r$ and $V$ change with time. In particular, we are given

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-54\pi \,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{s},
$$

and we want to find $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}$ when $r=3\,\text{cm}.$

To start, let's write down the volume formula for the sphere and then differentiate it using implicit differentiation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & =\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}r}(\frac{4}{3}\pi {r}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi {r}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now we can substitute the given information $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-54\pi $ and $r=3,$ and solve for $\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-54\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 4\pi (3)^{2} \\ -54\pi  & =\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t}\cdot 36\pi  \\ \frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}t} & =-1.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the radius of the sphere is decreasing at a rate of $1.5\text{ cm/s}$ when the radius is $3\,\text{cm}.$

questions.problem:
The table below gives the values of a positive, continuous function $f(x)$ and its derivative ${f}^{′}(x)$ over the closed interval $[1,9].$
Using a right Riemann sum with $4$ equal subintervals, estimate the arc length of the curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=1$ and $x=9.$

| $x$ | $1$ | $3$ | $5$ | $7$ | $9$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $4$ | $5$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\sqrt{2}$ | $1$ |
| ${f}^{′}(x)$ | $4\sqrt{5}$ | $0$ | $\sqrt{3}$ | $0$ | $3\sqrt{7}$ |

*Hint: The arc length of a smooth curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ is given by*

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the hint, we have that the arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=1$ and $x=9$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{1}^{9}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $g(x)=\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}.$ The (regular) step size $Δx$ is given by 

$$
Δx=\frac{9-1}{4}=2.
$$

We can approximate the integral above using a *right* Riemann sum with $4$ equal subintervals and step size $Δx$ as follows:

$$
{\int }_{1}^{9}g(x)\,\text{d}x≈(g(3)+g(5)+g(7)+g(9))\cdot Δx
$$

Now, we set up a table with values of $g(x)$ at each point:

| $x$ | $1$ | $3$ | $5$ | $7$ | $9$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}^{′}(x)$ | $4\sqrt{5}$ | $0$ | $\sqrt{3}$ | $0$ | $3\sqrt{7}$ |
| $g(x)=\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}$ | $9$ | $1$ | $2$ | $1$ | $8$ |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our arc length:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{1}^{9}g(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ≈(g(3)+g(5)+g(7)+g(9))\cdot Δx \\  & =(1+2+1+8)\cdot 2 \\  & =12\cdot 2 \\  & =24\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Approximate the value of $\sqrt{37}$ using the tangent line approximation of $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$ at $x=36.$
questions.worked_solution:
The tangent line approximation of $f(x)$ at the point $x=a$ is

$$
L(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a).
$$

In our case, we have $a=36,$ which gives

$$
L(x)=f(36)+{f}^{′}(36)(x-36).
$$

Let's compute $f(36)$ and ${f}^{′}(36)$ in the expression above. Evaluating the function, we get

$$
f(36)=\sqrt{36}=6,
$$

and computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\sqrt{x})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}},\end{aligned}
$$

which in turn gives

$$
{f}^{′}(36)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{36}}=\frac{1}{12}.
$$

So, the tangent line approximation is

$$
\begin{aligned}L(x)=6+\frac{1}{12}(x-36).\end{aligned}
$$

We can approximate $\sqrt{37}$ by evaluating the tangent line approximation at $x=37.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{37} & ≈L(37) \\  & =6+\frac{1}{12}(37-36) \\  & =6+\frac{1}{12} \\  & =\frac{73}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider a right triangle inscribed in a semicircle of radius
$6.$ If the hypotenuse of the triangle lies along the diameter of the semicircle, what is the greatest possible perimeter of the triangle?
questions.worked_solution:
We first draw a picture of the situation:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14188718/assets/417b284c87f735eb0c33f2369262b1548f9c54ff27ecbeb7880e91e9bc847f31.png)

Let's call $l$ the length of one of the legs. By the Pythagorean theorem, the length of the other leg is $\sqrt{144-{l}^{2}}.$

Therefore, the perimeter is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}P(l) & =12+l+\sqrt{144-{l}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $l$ is the length of a leg of a right triangle whose hypotenuse is $12,$ the permitted range of $l$ is $0<l<12.$

We want to maximize $P(l),$ so we need to compute the critical points. Taking the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(l) & =1+\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{-2l}{\sqrt{144-{l}^{2}}} \\  & =1-\frac{l}{\sqrt{144-{l}^{2}}},\end{aligned}
$$

and solving ${P}^{′}(l)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{′}(l) & =0 \\ 1-\frac{l}{\sqrt{144-{l}^{2}}} & =0 \\ \frac{l}{\sqrt{144-{l}^{2}}} & =1 \\ \sqrt{144-{l}^{2}} & =l \\ 144-{l}^{2} & ={l}^{2} \\ 2{l}^{2} & =144 \\ {l}^{2} & =72 \\ l & =6\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

All that's left now is to confirm that $l=6\sqrt{2}$ does indeed give a maximum value of $P(l).$ To do this, we use the first derivative test. We write up a table of values:

| Interval | $(0,6\sqrt{2})$ | $6\sqrt{2}$ | $(6\sqrt{2},12)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $1$ | $$ | $9$ |
| ${P}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $P$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |

So, $l=6\sqrt{2}$ does indeed give a maximum, and the perimeter of the resulting triangle will be the largest possible.

Therefore, the greatest perimeter that a triangle can have is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(6\sqrt{2}) & =12+6\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{144-(6\sqrt{2})^{2}} \\  & =12+6\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{144-72} \\  & =12+6\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{72} \\  & =12+6\sqrt{2}+6\sqrt{2} \\  & =12+12\sqrt{2} \\  & =12(1+\sqrt{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

The graph of the function $y={f}^{′}(x)$, the derivative of $y=f(x)$, is shown above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y={f}^{″}(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, if we denote $g(x)={f}^{′}(x)$ then ${f}^{″}(x)={g}^{′}(x).$ So, we need to sketch the graph of $y={g}^{′}(x)$ given the graph of $y=g(x),$ as usual.

Notice the following:

- At the stationary points, where the tangent line to $y=g(x)$ is parallel to the $x$-axis, we have ${g}^{′}(x)=0.$

- When $g(x)$ is increasing, we have ${g}^{′}(x)>0.$

- When $g(x)$ is decreasing, we have ${g}^{′}(x)<0.$

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below. Note that the stationary points were identified (approximately) from the graph of $y={g}^{′}(x)$:

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,-1)$ | $-1$ | $(-1,0)$ | $0$ | $(0,1)$ | $1$ | $(1,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $g$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |
| ${g}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |

Additionally, the function $y=g(x)$ has inflection points at $x≈-0.5$ and $x≈0.5.$ At the inflection points, we have ${g}^{″}(x)=0,$ so the tangent to the graph of $y={g}^{′}(x)$ must be parallel to the $x$-axis at $x≈-0.5$ and $x≈0.5.$

We don't know the exact values of ${g}^{′}(-0.5)$ and ${g}^{′}(0.5)$, but from the graph of $y=g(x)$ we find that the slope of the tangents to ${g}^{′}(x)$ at $x≈-0.5$ and $x≈0.5$ are negative and positive, respectively. 

Therefore, the graph of $y={g}^{′}(x)={f}^{″}(x)$ may look as shown below.
